doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
title: Rabbit Hodges and great communicators
summary: Mandel calls Johnny Hodges his favorite player and says Hodges, Getz, Lester Young, Parker and Louis had nothing between their thoughts and the listener.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: [laughs] Now to do that kind of…
Oh, good God, my favorite player I think of all of them.
I would say that you could, that he was probably Ellington’s greatest soloists, you know I mean some people would argue that, but you’d have to make a pretty serious argument.

Well, he was another one that was the great communicator; it was like there was nothing between his brain and your brain. There was no saxophone, there was no pads, no mechanism, it just went like right from where he was thinking right to your brain. It was something very few have been gifted with, Stan Getz had it, Lester Young certainly had it,
Charlie Parker had it and there's a few others but you know what, out of all the great jazz players there aren't that many that had that particular thing. Louis [Armstrong] of course had it.
Where you’re not conscious of the physical limitations of the instrument.

Yeah, there's absolutely no, there's no instrument between them and you and that's, that's I guess what I mean. You’re not conscious of it unless they mention it, they’re able to move you because there's nothing in-between.
